slides.title: MeetingToM: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs on Theory-of-Mind Reasoning in Multi-Party Meetings
slides.tldr: BENCHMARK FOR THEORY-OF-MIND REASONING IN MULTI-PARTY MEETINGS
slides.highlight: This work introduces MeetingToM to evaluate multimodal models on social behavior reasoning, specifically targeting addressee understanding and group-level consensus, which aligns with HyECHO's focus on addressee modeling and group norms.

card.one_liner: MeetingToM evaluates MLLMs' ability to reason about latent social states and group dynamics in multi-party meetings.
card.key_idea: A hierarchical benchmark featuring three tasks: subject-level mental state prediction, dyadic-level addressee/attitude inference, and group-level consensus reasoning, specifically targeting 'pseudo-consensus' where verbal agreement masks dissent.
card.evaluation: Evaluated proprietary (GPT-5, Gemini-3 Pro) and open-source (Qwen) MLLMs on 1,800 clips from the AMI Corpus using accuracy and Macro-F1; humans significantly outperform models.
card.limitation: Limited to English-language meetings, short video segments (5s/50s) rather than full meetings, and lacks direct participant self-reported mental states.

slides.title: Imitation of Arm Gestures by the Semi-Humanoid Robot NICO
slides.tldr: HUMAN ARM GESTURE IMITATION FOR SEMI-HUMANOID ROBOTS
slides.highlight: This work develops a system for a semi-humanoid robot to imitate human arm gestures using MediaPipe pose-estimation, contributing to the development of embodied social robots for RwB.

card.one_liner: A system for the NICO robot to imitate human arm gestures using monocular RGB input.
card.key_idea: Uses MediaPipe for 3D landmark extraction and analytical geometry to compute joint angles, which are then linearly mapped to NICO's specific motor configurations.
card.evaluation: Tested with six participants on 11 poses across three viewing angles. Results show moderate accuracy for most joints but high error for forearm rotation.
card.limitation: Significant reconstruction errors occur during forearm rotation and complex poses involving self-occlusion or extreme wrist flexion.

slides.title: How Reliable Are Multimodal Signals of Conversational State? Evidence from Remote Dyadic Collaborative Tasks
slides.tldr: EVALUATING MULTIMODAL SIGNALS FOR CONVERSATIONAL STATE
slides.highlight: This work evaluates the reliability of interactional, acoustic, and linguistic features for predicting cognitive load and power roles, which is relevant to HyECHO's focus on multimodal social perception and engagement.

card.one_liner: Multimodal signals of conversational state often lack generalizability and reliability once speaker identity is controlled.
card.key_idea: A three-dimensional framework evaluating predictive accuracy, cross-task generalizability, and test-retest reliability across interactional, acoustic, and linguistic features in remote dyadic collaborative tasks.
card.evaluation: Tested on AVCAffe dataset (53 dyads, 9 tasks) using Random Forest, LODO/LOCO cross-validation, and ICC. Results show linguistic features predict best but generalize poorly.
card.limitation: Conversational power prediction remained near chance, and results may vary for in-person or multi-party interactions beyond dyadic settings.

slides.title: Modeling turn-taking with distant viewing: investigating silence thresholds in human and AI-generated discourse
slides.tldr: SILENCE THRESHOLDS IN HUMAN AND AI DISCOURSE
slides.highlight: This study analyzes silence gaps in human and AI-generated audiovisual material, contributing to the understanding of turn-taking and engagement for HyECHO.

card.one_liner: Study compares silence gaps in human-led sitcoms versus AI-generated synthetic podcasts.
card.key_idea: Analysis of silence thresholds and gaps across speaker gender and production settings using fundamental-frequency estimation via Praat.
card.evaluation: Analyzed 30 US sitcoms and 51 Google NotebookLM synthetic podcasts; metrics focused on silence gap duration.

slides.title: Motion Primitive Discovery in a Humanoid Robot via Self-Organising Maps for Phase Recognition
slides.tldr: MOTOR PRIMITIVE DISCOVERY FOR PHASE RECOGNITION
slides.highlight: This work proposes an architecture for motor primitive discovery and online phase recognition in a humanoid robot, which is relevant to RwB's focus on human-robot interaction.

card.one_liner: A two-level MNS-inspired architecture for online movement phase recognition in a humanoid robot.
card.key_idea: Two Self-Organising Maps (SOMs) discover arm and hand motion primitives, which an Echo State Network (ESN) temporally integrates to recognize movement phases.
card.evaluation: Evaluated on 4,200 simulated NICO robot trials across seven actions; achieved 93.9% phase recognition accuracy using only SOM primitive descriptors.
card.limitation: Trained and evaluated only on the robot's own actions; lacks cross-embodiment mirroring for observing other agents.

slides.title: SpEmoC: A Balanced Speaker-Segment Multimodal Emotion Benchmark
slides.highlight: This work introduces a balanced multimodal dataset of synchronized visual, audio, and textual clips for emotion recognition, supporting HyECHO's goals in multimodal social perception.

card.one_liner: SpEmoC is a large-scale, class-balanced multimodal emotion benchmark for conversational speaking segments from movies and TV.
card.key_idea: A hybrid pipeline using pretrained text/audio models with KL-divergence logit fusion and human validation to curate 30k balanced, synchronized multimodal clips.
card.evaluation: Benchmarked five SOTA models (e.g., EMOE, TCL-MAP) via in-domain, cross-dataset, and low-data tests; results show significantly reduced imbalance gaps compared to MELD/CAER.
card.limitation: Demographic attributes are approximate as they are inferred from visual content using a pretrained model.

slides.title: Differentiable Logic Programming to Mitigate Reasoning Shortcuts in Neurosymbolic Systems
slides.tldr: MITIGATING REASONING SHORTCUTS IN NEUROSYMBOLIC SYSTEMS
slides.highlight: This work proposes a differentiable logic programming method to reduce constraint satisfaction and cognition shortcuts in neurosymbolic systems. It is relevant to MIMIC's use of neuro-symbolic agent models for societal-scale simulation.

card.one_liner: A differentiable logic programming method that reduces reasoning shortcuts in neurosymbolic systems using matrix-based semantics.
card.key_idea: Uses matrix-based differentiable logic programming with unified rule/constraint encoding and one-to-one grounding of neural outputs to logical atoms to prevent semantically incorrect mappings.
card.evaluation: Evaluated on MNIST variants; compared against soft probability distribution methods. Results show significant reduction in constraint satisfaction and cognition shortcuts.
